sections.name: The Neuron
tips: Exam-style questions from Phineas's kit for this deck. Read every choice before you pick: the wrong ones are common mix-ups.

questions.stem: Maria's neurologist explains that the fatty coating around her axons is breaking down, slowing her neural signals and making walking difficult. Maria most likely has:
questions.exp: MS is the breakdown of the myelin sheath (demyelination). Myasthenia gravis is the trap: it blocks acetylcholine receptors at the muscles and doesn't damage myelin.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the all-or-none principle?
options: Once threshold is reached, a neuron fires completely; below threshold it does not fire at all.
A stronger stimulus causes a neuron to fire with greater intensity.
A neuron must receive signals from all of its dendrites before it can fire.
A neuron releases either all of its neurotransmitters or none during reuptake.
questions.exp: A neuron's firing strength never changes. It either reaches threshold and fires fully, or it doesn't fire.

questions.stem: A new drug stops the sending neuron from reabsorbing leftover neurotransmitters in the synapse. Which process is the drug blocking?
questions.exp: Reuptake is the sending neuron reabsorbing leftover neurotransmitters. SSRIs work by blocking it.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes the path of a signal through a single neuron?
questions.exp: Dendrites detect the message, the soma decides to fire, the impulse travels down the axon, and terminal buttons release neurotransmitters.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the function of glial cells?
options: They support, nourish, and protect neurons.
They carry electrical impulses down the axon.
They form the gap between two neurons.
questions.exp: Glia are support cells ("glue"). They don't send the signal themselves.

questions.stem: Antibodies in Jordan's body are blocking his muscles' receptor sites for acetylcholine, and his muscles are growing weak. Jordan most likely has:
questions.exp: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder that blocks or destroys ACh receptors at the muscles. MS is the trap: it attacks myelin.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why neurons use chemical messengers to communicate with each other?
options: Neurons are physically connected, so chemicals flow directly between them.
The myelin sheath blocks electrical signals from reaching the dendrites.
Dendrites can only detect electrical signals, not chemical ones.
A small gap separates neurons, so neurotransmitters carry the signal across the synapse.
questions.exp: Neurons never touch. The electrical impulse stops at the terminal buttons, and neurotransmitters cross the synaptic gap.

questions.stem: Immediately after firing, a neuron will not fire again no matter how much it is stimulated. Which of the following best describes this?
options: It is at resting potential and waiting for stimulation.
It is in the refractory period and recovering.
Its myelin sheath has been damaged.
questions.exp: The refractory period is the recovery time after firing, like waiting for a toilet to refill before you can flush again.

questions.stem: Where are neurotransmitters stored before they are released into the synapse?
options: In vesicles inside the terminal buttons
questions.exp: Vesicles are tiny sacs in the terminal buttons that hold neurotransmitters until the neuron fires.

sections.name: Neurotransmitters
tips: Exam-style questions from Phineas's kit for this deck. Read every choice before you pick: the wrong ones are common mix-ups.

questions.stem: Ella has been diagnosed with depression. Her doctor prescribes a medication that keeps serotonin in the synapse longer. Which type of drug is this?
questions.exp: SSRI = selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor. Blocking reuptake leaves more serotonin in the synapse.

questions.stem: A patient with Parkinson's disease has tremors and trouble starting movements. A shortage of which neurotransmitter is most responsible?
questions.exp: Low dopamine → Parkinson's. High dopamine → schizophrenia.

questions.stem: Excess activity of which neurotransmitter has been linked to schizophrenia?
questions.exp: Too much dopamine is linked to schizophrenia; too little to Parkinson's.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the role of GABA?
options: It is the main excitatory neurotransmitter and is involved in memory.
It sends hunger signals to the brain.
It is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter and calms the nervous system.
It is the body's natural painkiller.
questions.exp: GABA is the brakes. Glutamate (the main excitatory one) is the trap.

questions.stem: Low levels of acetylcholine are most closely associated with which disorder?
questions.exp: ACh helps with memory and movement; too little is linked to Alzheimer's. Parkinson's is dopamine.

questions.stem: After finishing a marathon, Kai feels euphoric and barely notices the blisters on his feet. Which neurotransmitter best explains this?
questions.exp: Endorphins are natural painkillers (runner's high). Substance P is the trap: it sends pain signals.

questions.stem: Which neurotransmitter is the brain's major excitatory neurotransmitter and, in excess, is linked to migraines?
questions.exp: Glutamate = go. Too much is linked to anxiety, OCD, and migraines.

questions.stem: Sam's doctor suspects his trouble focusing is related to low levels of a chemical that also drives the fight-or-flight response. Which one?
questions.exp: Norepinephrine handles fight-or-flight plus focus and attention; low levels are linked to ADHD and depression.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly pairs a neurotransmitter with its function?
questions.exp: ACh = action (muscles) and memory. Serotonin is mood, endorphins relieve pain, and GABA is inhibitory.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the difference between excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters?
options: Excitatory ones work only in the brain; inhibitory ones work only in the spinal cord.
Excitatory ones make the receiving neuron more likely to fire; inhibitory ones make it less likely to fire.
Excitatory ones are hormones; inhibitory ones are neurotransmitters.
Excitatory ones speed up reuptake; inhibitory ones slow it down.
questions.exp: Excite = go, inhibit = stop. It's about the next neuron's chance of firing.

sections.name: Nervous & Endocrine Systems
tips: Exam-style questions from Phineas's kit for this deck. Read every choice before you pick: the wrong ones are common mix-ups.

questions.stem: While hiking, Leah spots a rattlesnake. Her heart races, her pupils dilate, and her digestion slows. Which division of the nervous system is responsible?
questions.exp: Sympathetic = stressed: fight, flight, or freeze.

questions.stem: After the snake slithers away, Leah's heart rate and breathing gradually return to normal. Which division is now most active?
questions.exp: Parasympathetic = rest and digest; it calms the body back down.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of the somatic nervous system at work?
options: Your heart speeding up before a test
Raising your hand to answer a question
Your pupils shrinking in bright light
questions.exp: Somatic = voluntary movement. The others are automatic, so they're autonomic.

questions.stem: When the doctor taps Luis's knee, his leg kicks before his brain even registers the tap. Which of the following best explains why the response is so fast?
options: The signal goes to the spinal cord and straight back out, without waiting for the brain.
Motor neurons are always faster than sensory neurons.
The cerebellum processes all reflexes instantly.
Hormones carry the signal directly to the leg.
questions.exp: Reflexes are directed by the spinal cord, which cuts out the trip to the brain.

questions.stem: Which type of neuron carries messages from the brain and spinal cord out to the muscles?
questions.exp: Efferent = exit. Afferent = arrive.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the role of interneurons?
options: They carry messages from the senses to the brain.
They carry messages from the brain to the muscles.
They relay messages between sensory and motor neurons within the brain and spinal cord.
They insulate axons to speed up signals.
questions.exp: Inter = in between. They connect sensory input to motor output inside the CNS.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains how the endocrine system differs from the nervous system?
options: Hormones travel along axons, so they act faster than neurotransmitters.
Hormones travel through the bloodstream, so they act more slowly but their effects last longer.
The endocrine system controls only voluntary movement.
Hormones act only inside the brain.
questions.exp: Blood is slower than nerves, but hormone effects linger.

questions.stem: Which gland is called the "master gland" because it signals other glands to release their hormones?
questions.exp: The pituitary regulates growth, stress, and reproduction and directs the other glands.

questions.stem: After a big Thanksgiving dinner, Aiden feels full and stops eating. Which hormone is most responsible for this signal?
questions.exp: Leptin = leave the table (full). Ghrelin = growling stomach (hungry).

questions.stem: A new mother feels a strong bond with her baby soon after giving birth. Which hormone plays the biggest role in this bonding?
questions.exp: Oxytocin is the bonding hormone: labor, mother–baby bonding, and close relationships.

questions.stem: Jet lag throws off Mia's sleep-wake cycle. Which hormone, released by the pineal gland in response to darkness, regulates this cycle?
questions.exp: Melatonin regulates the circadian rhythm and helps you sleep.

questions.stem: During a scary movie, Ben's adrenal glands release a hormone that raises his heart rate and blood sugar. Which hormone is it?
questions.exp: Adrenaline from the adrenal glands powers the fight-or-flight energy surge.

sections.name: The Brain
tips: Exam-style questions from Phineas's kit for this deck. Read every choice before you pick: the wrong ones are common mix-ups.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes what Phineas Gage's injury taught psychologists?
options: The frontal lobe plays a major role in personality and controlling behavior.
The occipital lobe is responsible for processing vision.
The cerebellum controls balance and coordination.
The temporal lobe is needed to understand speech.
questions.exp: After the rod went through his prefrontal cortex, Gage became impulsive, profane, and irritable: his personality changed, not his movement or senses.

questions.stem: Which of the following scenarios best illustrates neuroplasticity?
options: A student drinks coffee to stay alert while studying.
A runner's heart rate speeds up during a race.
After a stroke, a patient regains the ability to walk through months of therapy as other brain areas take over.
A person blinks when dust blows toward their eyes.
questions.exp: Plasticity is the brain reorganizing itself. The others are a drug effect, the sympathetic system, and a reflex.

questions.stem: Which of the following functions is most closely associated with the limbic system?
options: Coordinating balance and fine motor movement
Regulating emotions, forming memories, and survival drives like hunger
questions.exp: Limbic = amygdala (emotion), hippocampus (memory), hypothalamus (drives). Breathing and heartbeat are the medulla, part of the brainstem.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the primary function of the cerebellum?
options: Coordinating voluntary movement, balance, and posture
Controlling hunger, thirst, and body temperature
questions.exp: The cerebellum ("little brain") handles balance, coordination, and learned motor skills.

questions.stem: Which part of the brain plays a crucial role in controlling arousal and attention, and if damaged could leave a person in a coma?
questions.exp: The reticular formation controls arousal and consciousness. The hypothalamus is the trap: it handles hunger, thirst, temperature, and the 4 Fs.

questions.stem: Which part of the brainstem is most involved in regulating the sleep-wake cycle?
questions.exp: The pons connects the spinal cord to the brain and helps regulate sleep. The medulla handles breathing and heartbeat.

questions.stem: A gymnast's fall damages her medulla. Which function is most at risk?
questions.exp: The medulla controls life-sustaining functions, which is why medulla damage can be fatal.

questions.stem: After a stroke, Mr. Lee understands everything his family says, but he speaks slowly in short, broken phrases like "want... coffee." Which area was most likely damaged?
questions.exp: Broca's = broken speech production, with understanding mostly intact.

questions.stem: After a head injury, Ana speaks fluently, but her sentences make little sense and she can't follow what others say. Which area was most likely damaged?
questions.exp: Wernicke's = understanding language. The speech flows but doesn't make sense.

questions.stem: Which lobe contains the somatosensory cortex, which processes touch, temperature, and pain?
questions.exp: The somatosensory cortex is in the parietal lobe, right behind the motor cortex (in the frontal lobe).

questions.stem: A tumor in the temporal lobe would most likely affect a person's:
questions.exp: The temporal lobe holds the auditory cortex and Wernicke's area.

questions.stem: A stroke damages the motor cortex in Tom's left hemisphere. Which of the following is most likely?
options: Weakness or paralysis on the left side of his body
Weakness or paralysis on the right side of his body
Loss of hearing in his left ear
questions.exp: Contralateral control: the left brain controls the right side of the body.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the role of the thalamus?
options: It relays incoming sensory information (except smell) to the right areas of the cortex.
questions.exp: The thalamus is the sensory switchboard. Smell is the one sense that skips it.

questions.stem: Which brain structure is most involved in fear and aggression?
questions.exp: The amygdala processes fear and aggression and triggers fight-or-flight.

questions.stem: After surgery, a patient remembers his childhood clearly but cannot form any new long-term memories. Which structure was most likely removed?
questions.exp: The hippocampus moves new information into long-term memory. Old memories are stored elsewhere, so they survive.

questions.stem: A rat stops eating after damage to part of its hypothalamus. Which part was most likely damaged?
questions.exp: Lateral = lunch (hunger). Damage to the ventromedial hypothalamus causes overeating instead.

questions.stem: Which part of the brain regulates body temperature, hunger, and thirst?
questions.exp: Hypothalamus: temperature, thirst, hunger, and sexual responses. Don't mix it up with the thalamus, the sensory relay.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the role of the prefrontal cortex?
options: Planning, judgment, decision making, and personality
questions.exp: The prefrontal cortex handles executive functions; it was Phineas Gage's injury.

questions.stem: A doctor wants to check for a tumor quickly by looking at the shape of a patient's brain structures, not their activity. Which scan fits best?
questions.exp: CT (and MRI) show structure. fMRI, PET, and EEG show activity.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to see which brain areas become more active when people look at photos of their friends, as precisely as possible. Which technique is best?
questions.exp: fMRI shows function through blood flow and is more precise than PET.

questions.stem: Which technique records brain waves through electrodes placed on the scalp and is often used to detect seizures?
questions.exp: EEG = electrical activity.

questions.stem: Doctors sometimes cut the corpus callosum in patients with severe epilepsy. Which of the following best describes the purpose of this surgery?
options: To speed up communication between the hemispheres
To keep seizures from spreading from one hemisphere to the other
To reduce activity in the frontal lobe
questions.exp: The corpus callosum connects the hemispheres. Cutting it stops seizure activity from crossing over.

questions.stem: Which statement about the two hemispheres is most accurate?
options: The right hemisphere controls the right side of the body.
Language is processed equally by both hemispheres.
The corpus callosum controls movement on both sides of the body.
The left hemisphere is usually dominant for language, and each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body.
questions.exp: Left = language. Each side of the brain controls the opposite side of the body.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why young children often recover better from brain injuries than adults do?
options: Children's brains are more plastic, so other areas can take over lost functions more easily.
Children can grow new neurons anywhere in the brain.
Children do not use their cerebral cortex yet.
Children's neurons do not have myelin.
questions.exp: Plasticity is greatest in childhood. Neurogenesis happens in only a couple of areas, so B is a trap.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly matches a brain structure with its function?
questions.exp: Hippocampus = memory, cerebellum = balance, amygdala = fear, occipital lobe = vision.

questions.stem: Which part of the brain is primarily responsible for processing visual information?
questions.exp: Occipital = optical, at the back of the brain.

sections.name: Vision
tips: Exam-style questions from Phineas's kit for this deck. Read every choice before you pick: the wrong ones are common mix-ups.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why it is hard to see colors in a dimly lit room?
options: Rods detect color only in bright light.
Cones need more light to work, and rods, which work in dim light, don't detect color.
The lens can't focus in dim light.
The optic nerve shuts off in darkness.
questions.exp: Rods = reduced light, black and white. Cones = color, need brighter light.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes the path of light through the eye?
questions.exp: Light enters through the cornea, passes the pupil, is focused by the lens, and lands on the retina.

questions.stem: Which theory best explains why a person with red-green color blindness has trouble telling red from green?
questions.exp: Trichromatic theory: red, green, and blue cones. Color blindness usually comes from impaired red or green cones.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a monocular depth cue?
options: Comparing the slightly different images from each eye
Using both eyes to judge how close something is
questions.exp: Linear perspective works with one eye. The other three all need both eyes (binocular).

questions.stem: Which Gestalt principle explains why you see the letters on a page as separate words rather than one long string?
questions.exp: Proximity: things close together get grouped together.

questions.stem: Every player on one team wears red, so you see them as one group separate from the team in blue. Which Gestalt principle is this?
questions.exp: Similarity: things that look alike get grouped together.

questions.stem: Which part of the eye changes shape to focus images on near or far objects?
questions.exp: That shape change is called accommodation.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes feature detectors?
options: Neurons in the visual cortex that respond to specific details like edges, angles, and movement
Cells in the retina that detect color
The muscle that controls pupil size
Neurons that carry signals from the eye to the brain
questions.exp: Feature detectors are in the visual cortex, not the eye.

questions.stem: In a painting, a distant mountain looks hazy and blurry, so viewers see it as far away. Which depth cue is the artist using?
questions.exp: Relative clarity: sharp objects seem close, hazy ones seem far.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes transduction in vision?
options: The lens bends light so it focuses on the retina.
Rods and cones in the retina convert light energy into neural impulses.
The optic nerve carries signals to the occipital lobe.
The iris controls how much light enters the eye.
questions.exp: Transduction = converting energy into neural signals, and it happens in the retina.

sections.name: Hearing, Smell, Taste, Touch & more
tips: Exam-style questions from Phineas's kit for this deck. Read every choice before you pick: the wrong ones are common mix-ups.

questions.stem: An older adult's eardrum and middle-ear bones are damaged, but the cochlea is healthy. What type of hearing loss is this, and can it be treated?
options: Conduction hearing loss; it can often be fixed with surgery
Sensorineural hearing loss; it cannot be reversed
Conduction hearing loss; it can never be treated
Sensorineural hearing loss; it can be fixed with surgery
questions.exp: Conduction = the parts that conduct sound (eardrum, ossicles). It's correctable. Sensorineural is the cochlea or auditory nerve.

questions.stem: Which treatment would most likely help someone whose hearing loss comes from damaged hair cells in the cochlea?
questions.exp: Hair-cell damage is sensorineural. A cochlear implant sends signals straight to the auditory nerve.

questions.stem: Two sounds are equally loud, but one is a high whistle and the other a low drum. What property of the sound waves is different?
questions.exp: Frequency = pitch. Amplitude = loudness, and the question says they're equally loud.

questions.stem: A gymnast can do a backflip with her eyes closed because she senses where her arms and legs are. Which sense makes this possible?
questions.exp: Kinesthesis senses the position of body parts. The vestibular sense is about the head's position and balance.

questions.stem: The smell of fresh cookies instantly brings back a vivid childhood memory. Which of the following best explains why?
options: Smell signals go straight to brain areas connected to the limbic system, which handles emotion and memory.
Smell is processed in the occipital lobe.
The thalamus amplifies smell signals before they reach the cortex.
Taste buds store memories of familiar foods.
questions.exp: Smell is the only sense that skips the thalamus. It connects directly to emotion and memory areas.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes gate control theory?
options: Pain is felt only when all four skin senses are activated at once.
The spinal cord has a neurological "gate" that can block pain signals or let them reach the brain.
The thalamus decides which pains are real.
Pain receptors stop firing after a few seconds.
questions.exp: Distraction or rubbing the spot can close the gate.

questions.stem: Years after losing his arm, Marcus still feels an itch in his missing hand. This is called:
questions.exp: The sensory cortex area for the missing limb is still active.

questions.stem: Whenever Priya hears a trumpet, she also sees the color orange. This is an example of:
questions.exp: Synesthesia is one sense triggering another. Sensory interaction is the trap: one sense influencing another, like smell and taste.

questions.stem: A person with prosopagnosia would have the most trouble:
questions.exp: Prosopagnosia = face blindness.

questions.stem: Jamal finds jalapeños unbearably hot, while his friend barely notices them. Jamal is most likely:
questions.exp: Supertasters have more taste buds and feel tastes and pain more intensely.

questions.stem: Which of the following is one of the five basic tastes?
questions.exp: The five are sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami. "Spicy" is actually pain.

sections.name: Sleep, Consciousness & Drugs
tips: Exam-style questions from Phineas's kit for this deck. Read every choice before you pick: the wrong ones are common mix-ups.

questions.stem: Which statement about sleep is most accurate?
options: Sleep is an altered state of consciousness, and the brain stays active even during sound sleep.
During sleep, the body and brain shut off until morning.
Only some people dream, and only on some nights.
Sleep is a period of dormancy for both the body and the brain.
questions.exp: Your slides: sleep is NOT dormancy; the brain is still active, and everyone dreams every night.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the circadian rhythm?
options: The order of the four sleep stages
A disorder in which people fall asleep suddenly
The body's biological clock: regular cycles on a 24-hour schedule, synced with day and night
questions.exp: Circadian rhythm = the biological clock on a 24-hour cycle.

questions.stem: Tia, 16, struggles in her first-period class but feels sharp by evening. Her grandfather is up at dawn and fades by dinner. Which of the following best explains this?
options: Tia has narcolepsy and her grandfather has insomnia.
Most teens are evening-energized, while most older adults are morning people.
Older adults don't have circadian rhythms.
Teens' body temperature is highest in the morning.
questions.exp: Teens and young adults improve across the day; older adults lose energy as the day goes on.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes body temperature across the day?
options: It is highest at night and lowest in the morning.
It stays the same all day.
It rises through the day, dips in the afternoon, and is lowest at night.
It is lowest in the afternoon and highest at night.
questions.exp: Body temperature increases throughout the day, dips in the afternoon, and is lowest at night.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an effect of sleep loss?
options: Lower risk of high blood pressure
Suppressed immune cell production and more colds
questions.exp: Sleep loss weakens the immune system, raises blood pressure risk, and hurts memory and reaction time.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why ongoing sleep loss is linked to obesity?
options: It raises leptin, which makes people hungrier.
It increases GABA, which slows metabolism.
It blocks the reuptake of dopamine.
It raises hunger-arousing ghrelin, lowers hunger-suppressing leptin, and increases fat cell production.
questions.exp: Ghrelin up, leptin down, more fat cells → greater risk of obesity.

questions.stem: A student who has been sleeping only four hours a night has trouble focusing in class and remembering what she studied. Which effect of sleep loss is this?
options: Diminished attentional focus and memory consolidation
questions.exp: Brain effects of sleep loss: less focus, weaker memory consolidation, higher risk of depression.

questions.stem: Darnell's wife notices that he stops breathing several times every night. Darnell most likely has:
questions.exp: Sleep apnea = you stop breathing in your sleep.

questions.stem: In the middle of a conversation, Rosa suddenly falls asleep without warning. She most likely has:
questions.exp: Narcolepsy = falling asleep spontaneously. Insomnia is the opposite: you can't sleep.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes night terrors?
options: Intense fear and screaming or crying during Stage 3, usually not remembered the next morning
Bad dreams that are remembered in detail the next morning
Suddenly falling asleep during the day
questions.exp: Night terrors are not nightmares: Stage 3, intense terror, no recollection in the morning.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes an agonist?
options: A drug that blocks the effects of a neurotransmitter
A drug that fits into receptors, mimics a neurotransmitter, and increases its effects
A drug that only affects the body, not the brain
The discomfort after stopping a drug
questions.exp: Agonist = acts like the neurotransmitter. Example: opiates mimic endorphins.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes an antagonist?
options: A drug that mimics a neurotransmitter and increases its effects
A drug made from the opium poppy
A drug that only works on hormones
A drug that blocks the effects of a neurotransmitter
questions.exp: Antagonist = against it. Your slides' example: cocaine blocking dopamine reuptake.

questions.stem: Cocaine produces alertness, euphoria, and motivation by:
questions.exp: Cocaine blocks dopamine reuptake, then comes a huge crash with anxiety, depression, and cravings.

questions.stem: People at a party get loud and do wild things after drinking, so some assume alcohol is a stimulant. Which of the following best explains why it is actually a depressant?
options: It blocks the reuptake of dopamine.
It distorts visual and auditory perception.
It intensifies GABA and reduces glutamate, slowing neural activity, reactions, and judgment.
questions.exp: Depressants reduce neural activity. Alcohol only seems like a stimulant because of how people act.

questions.stem: A doctor prescribes a "downer" to treat a patient's insomnia. It increases GABA and has effects similar to alcohol. Which type of drug is it most likely?
questions.exp: Barbiturates/sedatives: "downers," used for insomnia, alcohol-like, increase GABA, and cause dependence.

questions.stem: Which drug mimics adrenaline, gives a sense of euphoria followed by a huge crash, and leads to a cycle of addiction?
questions.exp: Amphetamines mimic epinephrine/adrenaline. Meth and ecstasy are forms.

questions.stem: Which substance is considered both a stimulant and a hallucinogen?
questions.exp: Ecstasy/MDMA is on your slides as a form of amphetamine and as a hallucinogen.

questions.stem: Heavy ecstasy use can permanently lower a person's mood and impair memory. Which of the following best explains why?
options: It increases GABA and slows neural activity.
It acts as an agonist for endorphins.
It blocks the reuptake of dopamine.
questions.exp: Ecstasy can damage serotonin-producing neurons → permanent deflation of mood and memory problems.

questions.stem: Which drug produces hallucinations and delusions like a psychotic state and can lead to paranoia and panic attacks?
questions.exp: LSD can result in psychosis, memory loss, paranoia, panic attacks, nightmares, and aggression.

questions.stem: THC, the active ingredient in marijuana, is most likely to produce:
options: A huge crash with strong cravings
Mild hallucinations, relaxation, and a distorted sense of time
questions.exp: THC: mild hallucinations, euphoria, relaxation, wellbeing, and time distortion.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why opioids such as heroin relieve pain?
options: They act as agonists for endorphins, reducing pain and increasing positive feelings.
They block the reuptake of dopamine.
They distort visual and auditory perception.
questions.exp: Opioids are endorphin agonists.

questions.stem: With continued opioid use, the brain stops producing its own dopamine and endorphins. This most directly leads to:
questions.exp: Opioids result in dependence, tolerance, withdrawal, and physiological and psychological addiction.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly matches a drug with its category?
questions.exp: Benzodiazepines are depressants, LSD is a hallucinogen, and codeine is an opioid.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the difference between substance use and substance abuse?
options: Use involves illegal drugs; abuse involves legal drugs.
Use doesn't interfere with daily functioning; abuse is a pattern that hurts functioning, can be dangerous, and leads to legal trouble.
Use happens daily; abuse happens only occasionally.
There is no difference between them.
questions.exp: Substance use = no interference with daily life. Substance abuse = it inhibits functioning.

questions.stem: Nina says, "I don't even enjoy it anymore, but I can't stop wanting it." This best describes:
questions.exp: Addiction: users want the drug more than they like the drug, and keep using despite consequences.

questions.stem: Withdrawal is best described as:
options: The discomfort and distress that follow stopping an addictive drug, which can be physiological and/or psychological
Needing more of a drug to get the same effect
Using a drug without it affecting daily life
The euphoria right after taking a drug
questions.exp: Withdrawal can be physiological, psychological, or both. "Needing more" is tolerance.

questions.stem: A person meets 7 of the DSM-5 criteria for substance use disorder. The disorder would be classified as:
questions.exp: Your slide: mild = 3, moderate = 4 or 5, severe = 6 or more.

questions.stem: Which of the following is one of the DSM-5 criteria for substance use disorder?
options: Using a substance once at a party
Wanting to cut down or stop using but not managing to
questions.exp: "Wanting to cut down or stop but not managing to" is criterion 2 on the slide's list of 11.

sections.name: Split Brain
tips: Exam-style questions from Phineas's kit for this deck. Read every choice before you pick: the wrong ones are common mix-ups.

questions.stem: A split-brain patient holds a hidden key in her left hand and can't see it. Asked what she is holding, which of the following is most likely?
options: She can't name it, but she can pick out the key with her left hand.
She can point to the key only with her right hand.
She can't identify it in any way.
questions.exp: Touch from the left hand goes to the right hemisphere, which can't speak but controls the left hand.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes what research on split-brain patients revealed?
options: Cutting the corpus callosum causes paralysis.
The two hemispheres specialize in different functions, such as language in the left hemisphere.
questions.exp: Split-brain studies showed lateralization, like language on the left side.

questions.stem: A split-brain patient looks at the center of the word HEART, so "HE" is in his left visual field and "ART" is in his right. Asked what word he saw, he will most likely say:
questions.exp: "ART" reaches the left hemisphere, which can speak. "HE" reaches only the right hemisphere, so he could point to it with his left hand but not say it.

sections.name: Mock exam
examTips: Turn the Timer on and answer every question without looking anything up.
Aim for about one minute per question. Flag hard ones and come back.
tips: A mix of exam-style questions from every deck in this unit.

questions.stem: Maria's neurologist explains that the fatty coating around her axons is breaking down, slowing her neural signals and making walking difficult. Maria most likely has:
questions.exp: MS is the breakdown of the myelin sheath (demyelination). Myasthenia gravis is the trap: it blocks acetylcholine receptors at the muscles and doesn't damage myelin.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the all-or-none principle?
options: A stronger stimulus causes a neuron to fire with greater intensity.
Once threshold is reached, a neuron fires completely; below threshold it does not fire at all.
A neuron must receive signals from all of its dendrites before it can fire.
A neuron releases either all of its neurotransmitters or none during reuptake.
questions.exp: A neuron's firing strength never changes. It either reaches threshold and fires fully, or it doesn't fire.

questions.stem: A new drug stops the sending neuron from reabsorbing leftover neurotransmitters in the synapse. Which process is the drug blocking?
questions.exp: Reuptake is the sending neuron reabsorbing leftover neurotransmitters. SSRIs work by blocking it.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes the path of a signal through a single neuron?
questions.exp: Dendrites detect the message, the soma decides to fire, the impulse travels down the axon, and terminal buttons release neurotransmitters.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the function of glial cells?
options: They carry electrical impulses down the axon.
They support, nourish, and protect neurons.
They form the gap between two neurons.
questions.exp: Glia are support cells ("glue"). They don't send the signal themselves.

questions.stem: Ella has been diagnosed with depression. Her doctor prescribes a medication that keeps serotonin in the synapse longer. Which type of drug is this?
questions.exp: SSRI = selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor. Blocking reuptake leaves more serotonin in the synapse.

questions.stem: A patient with Parkinson's disease has tremors and trouble starting movements. A shortage of which neurotransmitter is most responsible?
questions.exp: Low dopamine → Parkinson's. High dopamine → schizophrenia.

questions.stem: Excess activity of which neurotransmitter has been linked to schizophrenia?
questions.exp: Too much dopamine is linked to schizophrenia; too little to Parkinson's.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the role of GABA?
options: It is the main excitatory neurotransmitter and is involved in memory.
It sends hunger signals to the brain.
It is the body's natural painkiller.
It is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter and calms the nervous system.
questions.exp: GABA is the brakes. Glutamate (the main excitatory one) is the trap.

questions.stem: Low levels of acetylcholine are most closely associated with which disorder?
questions.exp: ACh helps with memory and movement; too little is linked to Alzheimer's. Parkinson's is dopamine.

questions.stem: While hiking, Leah spots a rattlesnake. Her heart races, her pupils dilate, and her digestion slows. Which division of the nervous system is responsible?
questions.exp: Sympathetic = stressed: fight, flight, or freeze.

questions.stem: After the snake slithers away, Leah's heart rate and breathing gradually return to normal. Which division is now most active?
questions.exp: Parasympathetic = rest and digest; it calms the body back down.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of the somatic nervous system at work?
options: Your heart speeding up before a test
Your pupils shrinking in bright light
Raising your hand to answer a question
questions.exp: Somatic = voluntary movement. The others are automatic, so they're autonomic.

questions.stem: When the doctor taps Luis's knee, his leg kicks before his brain even registers the tap. Which of the following best explains why the response is so fast?
options: Motor neurons are always faster than sensory neurons.
The signal goes to the spinal cord and straight back out, without waiting for the brain.
The cerebellum processes all reflexes instantly.
Hormones carry the signal directly to the leg.
questions.exp: Reflexes are directed by the spinal cord, which cuts out the trip to the brain.

questions.stem: Which type of neuron carries messages from the brain and spinal cord out to the muscles?
questions.exp: Efferent = exit. Afferent = arrive.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes what Phineas Gage's injury taught psychologists?
options: The occipital lobe is responsible for processing vision.
The frontal lobe plays a major role in personality and controlling behavior.
The cerebellum controls balance and coordination.
The temporal lobe is needed to understand speech.
questions.exp: After the rod went through his prefrontal cortex, Gage became impulsive, profane, and irritable: his personality changed, not his movement or senses.

questions.stem: Which of the following scenarios best illustrates neuroplasticity?
options: A student drinks coffee to stay alert while studying.
After a stroke, a patient regains the ability to walk through months of therapy as other brain areas take over.
A runner's heart rate speeds up during a race.
A person blinks when dust blows toward their eyes.
questions.exp: Plasticity is the brain reorganizing itself. The others are a drug effect, the sympathetic system, and a reflex.

questions.stem: Which of the following functions is most closely associated with the limbic system?
options: Coordinating balance and fine motor movement
Regulating emotions, forming memories, and survival drives like hunger
questions.exp: Limbic = amygdala (emotion), hippocampus (memory), hypothalamus (drives). Breathing and heartbeat are the medulla, part of the brainstem.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the primary function of the cerebellum?
options: Controlling hunger, thirst, and body temperature
Coordinating voluntary movement, balance, and posture
questions.exp: The cerebellum ("little brain") handles balance, coordination, and learned motor skills.

questions.stem: Which part of the brain plays a crucial role in controlling arousal and attention, and if damaged could leave a person in a coma?
questions.exp: The reticular formation controls arousal and consciousness. The hypothalamus is the trap: it handles hunger, thirst, temperature, and the 4 Fs.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why it is hard to see colors in a dimly lit room?
options: Rods detect color only in bright light.
The lens can't focus in dim light.
The optic nerve shuts off in darkness.
Cones need more light to work, and rods, which work in dim light, don't detect color.
questions.exp: Rods = reduced light, black and white. Cones = color, need brighter light.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes the path of light through the eye?
questions.exp: Light enters through the cornea, passes the pupil, is focused by the lens, and lands on the retina.

questions.stem: Which theory best explains why a person with red-green color blindness has trouble telling red from green?
questions.exp: Trichromatic theory: red, green, and blue cones. Color blindness usually comes from impaired red or green cones.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a monocular depth cue?
options: Comparing the slightly different images from each eye
Using both eyes to judge how close something is
questions.exp: Linear perspective works with one eye. The other three all need both eyes (binocular).

questions.stem: Which Gestalt principle explains why you see the letters on a page as separate words rather than one long string?
questions.exp: Proximity: things close together get grouped together.

questions.stem: An older adult's eardrum and middle-ear bones are damaged, but the cochlea is healthy. What type of hearing loss is this, and can it be treated?
options: Sensorineural hearing loss; it cannot be reversed
Conduction hearing loss; it can never be treated
Conduction hearing loss; it can often be fixed with surgery
Sensorineural hearing loss; it can be fixed with surgery
questions.exp: Conduction = the parts that conduct sound (eardrum, ossicles). It's correctable. Sensorineural is the cochlea or auditory nerve.

questions.stem: Which treatment would most likely help someone whose hearing loss comes from damaged hair cells in the cochlea?
questions.exp: Hair-cell damage is sensorineural. A cochlear implant sends signals straight to the auditory nerve.

questions.stem: Two sounds are equally loud, but one is a high whistle and the other a low drum. What property of the sound waves is different?
questions.exp: Frequency = pitch. Amplitude = loudness, and the question says they're equally loud.

questions.stem: A gymnast can do a backflip with her eyes closed because she senses where her arms and legs are. Which sense makes this possible?
questions.exp: Kinesthesis senses the position of body parts. The vestibular sense is about the head's position and balance.

questions.stem: The smell of fresh cookies instantly brings back a vivid childhood memory. Which of the following best explains why?
options: Smell signals go straight to brain areas connected to the limbic system, which handles emotion and memory.
Smell is processed in the occipital lobe.
The thalamus amplifies smell signals before they reach the cortex.
Taste buds store memories of familiar foods.
questions.exp: Smell is the only sense that skips the thalamus. It connects directly to emotion and memory areas.
